plain: The city's main account for everyday services like police, fire, parks and libraries, paid for mostly by local taxes. It is the part of the budget the City Council has the most freedom to spend.

Money the city can count on only once, such as savings left over from last year or a temporary federal grant. Using it to pay for costs that come back every year leaves a hole in the next year's budget.
The amount by which the city's regular yearly costs are bigger than its regular yearly income. One-time money can cover it for a year, but it comes back until costs are cut or income goes up.

A deposit into the city's rainy-day savings, kept for emergencies and economic downturns. Skipping the deposit makes one year's budget easier to balance but leaves the savings further below the city's own target.

Short for actuarially determined contribution: the yearly payment into the city employees' pension fund that the pension system's actuary says is required to pay for promised retirement benefits. San Diego has paid the full amount every year since FY2006, so each budget includes it in full.
A fund for a service that customers pay for directly, such as water or sewer service. The fees go into that fund and can be spent only on that service, not on the city's general costs.
A fund that holds money the law sets aside for a specific purpose, such as a grant for a certain program or a tax meant for a certain use. It cannot be spent on other things.
The city's plan for building and repairing long-lasting things like roads, buildings, pipes and parks. Projects can take several years, so the money is tracked project by project.
The amount the city has promised to pay, such as retirement benefits, that is not yet covered by money set aside. It is an estimate that changes with investment returns and with the assumptions used.
The share of a pension fund's promised benefits that it has money set aside to pay. A ratio of 100% would mean the promises are fully covered.
Savings the city keeps for emergencies and economic downturns. The city has a policy target for how large the savings should be.
A score from 0 to 100 for how good a stretch of road is, based on a survey of cracks and wear. A higher score means a road in better shape.
